definition: Buttress means to support or strengthen something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word buttress. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know buttress should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Volunteers buttressed the bookmobile's overloaded shelves with steel brackets before the winter routes began.
Propping up is the quick, temporary version — a broom handle under a sagging shelf — and it stops short of buttressing, which builds lasting support into the thing.
Fortify goes further than buttress — buttressing strengthens a weak point so it holds, while fortifying hardens the whole thing against outright attack.

Reinforce is the general engineering word for adding strength anywhere — more steel in the concrete, more staff on a shift, more evidence behind a claim. Buttress is more pointed: it braces one particular thing that faces real pressure, standing behind it and shouldering part of the strain.

To shore up is emergency propping for something already failing — a levee about to breach, a firm about to fold. Buttress does not wait for failure: you buttress something while it is still sound so that it can bear more when the pressure comes.

Bolster boosts confidence, morale, or numbers as readily as structures — a good scrimmage bolsters a team's nerve. Buttress is the firmer, more structural word: it implies bracing a thing against real pressure, whether that thing is a wall, a case, or a nervous witness.

Shaky at the podium, the freshman senator was buttressed by her staff's binder: every question from the panel met a tabbed page, and by the second hour her voice had stopped wavering.

Buttress is the exact word because it means to support or strengthen something so it can hold up under pressure — the binder does not replace her answers or give them for her; it stands behind her and takes part of the strain, which is precisely the job the word names.
Buttress does double duty: literal masonry and figurative support for claims, cases, and confidence, and it always suggests bracing something that faces real pressure.
Its unit-mate stabilize stops a thing from getting worse; buttress adds strength so it can bear more.
In casual speech, back up or support is plainer.

The mountain observatory's dome had stood for ninety years, but the new sky survey called for a heavier telescope and a heavier mount.
Rather than wait to see how the old ring wall handled the change, the engineers chose to buttress it before installation began.
Steel ribs now rise against the wall's outer face, each one angled to take a share of the new weight and the wind.
The wall itself was never cracked or failing; the ribs are there because the pressure on it is about to grow.
When the first winter storms loaded the dome with ice, the ring wall carried it without a groan, the ribs shouldering the strain exactly as drawn.
